```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Load data
diamonds <- read.csv("dia.csv")

# Fit model M1
model_m1 <- lm(log(price) ~log(x) , data = diamonds)


# Model summary
 summary(model_m1)

```

a.  

From summary,
$M1: \log(\text{price}) = 5.93 \cdot \log(x) - 2.46$

From Jeweller, $price \propto weight^{log1.21/log1.10}$,then
$price \propto weight^{2}$

By geometrical background and constant density $weight \propto x^{3}$

Then, combine both the information from Jeweller and geometrical
background, $price \propto x^{6}$, taking log, we get
$log(price) \propto 6logx$

This theoretical coefficient of 6 is very close to the estimated
coefficient 5.93 from model M1, suggesting that the fitted model is
reasonable.

b.  

From Jeweller, $price \propto weight^{2}$

By geometrical background and constant density $weight \propto x \cdot y \cdot z$

Combine these two and taking log, we get
$log(price)\propto 2log(x)+2log(y)+2log(z)$

Then, approximate values for $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$ and $\beta_3$ are both
2.

  

```{r, echo=FALSE}
model_m2 <- lm(log(price) ~ log(x) + log(y) + log(z), data = diamonds)

summary(model_m2)
```

c.  

$\mathbb{E}[log(Price_j)]$ =
$\beta_0+\beta_1log(xj)+\beta_2log(y_j)+\beta_3log(z_j)$

To test $H_0$:$\beta_1=0$ vs $H_1$:$\beta_1 \not= 0$ we use a t-test.
The number of units of observation in the dataset is $n=607$ and the M2
model has $p=4$ parameters. Hence, under $H_0$, the $T$-statistic,
defined as
$\frac{\widehat{\beta_1}}{{\rm std.error}(\widehat{\beta_1})}$ has a
$t$-distribution on $n-p=607-4 = 603$ degrees of freedom. As is listed
in the 2nd row of the table of coefficients, the observed value of the
$T$-statistic is $T_{\rm obs} = -0.200$ which has a $p$-value of
$0.842$. Thus there is insufficient evidence at the 5% level to reject
the null hypothesis that $\beta_1=0$. We conclude that including log(x)
does not have significant improvement after accounting for log(y) and
log(z) in the model. Hence we do not include log(x) term in the model.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
anova(model_m2)
```

d.  

$H_0$: log(x) provides no additional explanatory power over the null
    model. $H_1$: log(x) contributes significant explanatory power over
    the null model. The test statistic is the F-statistic, which under
    $H_0$ follows an F(1,605) distribution. Observed F-value = $1.23 \times 10^{4}$
    and corresponding p-value that is less than 0.001. We reject $H_0$.
    Hence, log(x) is highly significant when added first to the model.

This result is not contradictory to part (c). The test in (c) examines
whether log(x) is significant after accounting for log(y) and log(z),
while sequential ANOVA tests whether log(x) is significant alone. The
high correlation between x, y, and z explains why log(x) appears
insignificant in part (c) but highly significant in sequential ANOVA.

e.  

From summary results of M2, estimated $\beta 1$=-0.162,
    $\beta 2$=4.39, $\beta 3$=1.78, while the theoretical
    coefficients are both 2. The estimated coefficients of model M2 are
    substantially different from the theoretically expected value of 2
    for all three predictors. The primary reason for these
    counter-intuitive results is strong multicollinearity between
    log(x), log(y), and log(z).

In the context of round diamonds, the physical dimensions x, y and z
(length, width, depth) are inherently highly correlated, as they all
describe the overall size of the stone. A diamond that is large in one
dimension will almost certainly be large in the others. This strong
linear dependence means the three log-transformed variables carry
largely overlapping information.

Numerically, this can be supported by high pairwise correlation
coefficients between log(x), log(y) and log(z). Graphically, the
scatterplot matrix of these variables would show strong linear
associations, visually confirming the severe multicollinearity that
distorts the individual slope estimates in M2.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
log_vars <- log(diamonds[, c("x", "y", "z")])
cor_matrix=cor(log_vars)
round(cor_matrix, 3)
cat('table1: correlations between pairs of log(x),log(y) and log(z)')
```

```{r,out.width="65%",fig.align='center', fig.cap="A scatterplot matrix of the three explanatory variables log(x), log(y) and log(z) from diamonds dataset. We see that each pair of log(x), log(y) and log(z) all have a strong linear relationship",echo=FALSE}

pairs(log(x) ~ log(y) + log(z), data = diamonds)
```

  

```{r,echo=FALSE}
model_m3 <- lm(log(price) ~ log(weight), data = diamonds)
```

  

```{r,echo=FALSE}
good <- diamonds[diamonds$cut == "Good", ]
verygood <- diamonds[diamonds$cut == "Very Good", ]
ideal <- diamonds[diamonds$cut == "Ideal", ]
```


```{r,out.width="65%",fig.align='center', fig.cap=" A scatterplot for log(weight) against log(price) for good cut dataset . The red line is the fitted regression line for for good cut dataset, and the blue line is the fitted line from model M3 using the full dataset.",echo=FALSE}
fit_good <- lm(log(price) ~ log(weight), data = good)
plot(log(price) ~ log(weight), data = good, main = "Good Cut", xlab = "log(weight) (in log(carat))", ylab = "log(price) (in log(US dollar))")
abline(fit_good, col = "red", lwd = 2)         
abline(model_m3, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```


```{r,out.width="65%",fig.align='center', fig.cap="A scatterplot for log(weight) against log(price) for very good cut dataset. The red line is the fitted regression line for very good cut dataset, and the blue line is the fitted line from model M3 using the full dataset.",echo=FALSE}
fit_vg <- lm(log(price) ~ log(weight), data = verygood)
plot(log(price) ~ log(weight), data = verygood,
     main = "Very Good Cut", xlab = "log(weight) (in log(carat))", ylab = "log(price) (in log(US dollar))")
abline(fit_vg, col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(model_m3, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```


```{r,out.width="65%",fig.align='center', fig.cap="A scatterplot for log(weight) against log(price) for ideal cut dataset. The red line is the fitted regression line for ideal cut dataset, and the blue line is the fitted line from model M3 using the full dataset.",echo=FALSE}
fit_ideal <- lm(log(price) ~ log(weight), data = ideal)
plot(log(price) ~ log(weight), data = ideal, main = "Ideal Cut", xlab = "log(weight) (in log(carat))", ylab = "log(price) (in log(US dollar))")
abline(fit_ideal, col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(model_m3, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

```

c.  

From the three plots for Good, Very Good and Ideal cut diamonds, we
    observe that: The regression lines for each cut group are similar in
    slope to each other and to the overall line from model M3. The
    intercepts differ slightly between the three cut groups. The
    relationship between log(price) and log(weight) is consistently
    linear across all levels of cut.

Merit of adding cut as a main effect: Adding cut as a main effect to
model M3 is beneficial.Because the intercepts differ between cut
categories, cut explains differences in the average price level at the
same weight. Including cut as a main effect improves the model fit by
accounting for these vertical shifts in price.

Merit of adding cut as main effect + interaction with log(weight):
Adding an interaction term between cut and log(weight) is not necessary
or beneficial.The slopes of the regression lines are nearly identical
across the three cut groups, meaning the relationship between price and
weight does not change across cut quality. The interaction term would
not improve the model meaningfully.

  

```{r,echo = FALSE}
model_main <- lm(log(price) ~ log(weight) + cut, data = diamonds)

anova(model_m3, model_main)
```

d.  

$H_0$: All coefficients for cut are zero. $H_1$: At least one
coefficient for cut is non-zero. The test statistic is the F-statistic,
which under $H_0$ follows an F(2,603) distribution. Observed F-value =
23.9 and corresponding p-value = $1.03 \times 10^{-10}$< 0.05. We reject $H_0$.
Hence, Cut is highly significant and we include Cut variable to the
model.

```{r,echo = FALSE}
model_interaction <- lm(log(price) ~ log(weight) + cut + log(weight) * cut, data = diamonds)

anova(model_main, model_interaction)
```

$H_0$: All coefficients for the interaction cut:log(weight) are zero,
given that main effects of cut and log(weight) are included. $H_1$: At least one interaction coefficient is non-zero , given that main effects of cut and log(weight) are included. 

The test statistic is the F-statistic, which under $H_0$ follows an F(2,601) distribution.
Observed F-value = 1.66 and corresponding p-value = 0.192 > 0.05. We do not have enough evidence to reject $H_0$. Hence, there is no significant evidence that the interaction improves the model, so we do not include the interaction term between cut and log(weight).

```{r,echo=FALSE}
M <- lm(log(price) ~ cut/log(weight), data = diamonds)
summary(M)

```

e.  

For Good cut: log(price)=$\beta_0 + \beta_1 log(weight)$ For Very Good
cut: log(price)=$(\beta_0+\delta_0)+(\beta_1+\delta_1) log(weight)$

For Ideal cut:
log(price)=$(\beta_0+\gamma_0)+(\beta_1+\gamma_1) log(weight)$

$\beta_0$ = intercept for Good cut  
$\beta_1$= slope for Good cut    
$\delta_0$= intercept difference for Very Good and good cut    
$\gamma_0$=intercept difference for Ideal and good cut  
$\delta_1$= slope difference for Very Good and good cut  
$\gamma_1$= slope difference for Ideal and
good cut   

least squares estimate: $\beta_0$= 8.48,  
$\gamma_0$= 0.107, $\delta_0$= 0.0528, $\beta_1$= 1.96 ,$\gamma_1$=
1.9330-1.9563=-0.0233, $\delta_1$= 2.0122-1.9563=0.0559

  

```{r, out.width="70%", fig.align='center', fig.cap="Residuals vs fitted values for model M4 (log(price) ~ log(weight) + cut), points colour-coded by diamond clarity.", echo=FALSE}
# Fit model M4
M4 <- lm(log(price) ~ log(weight) + cut, data = diamonds)

# Plot residuals vs fitted values, colour by clarity
plot(fitted(M4), resid(M4), 
     col = as.factor(diamonds$clarity), 
     pch = 16, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted (M4)")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = levels(as.factor(diamonds$clarity)),
       col = 1:length(levels(as.factor(diamonds$clarity))), pch = 16)
```

a.  

The residuals show a clear pattern separated by colour (clarity).
Different clarity levels cluster in distinct regions of residual values.
Red(VS) points cluster above the red line and black(SI) points cluster
below the red line. This indicates that clarity is strongly associated
with the remaining variation in price not explained by log(weight) and
cut. Therefore, adding clarity as an additional predictor is likely to
significantly improve the model by explaining the structured residual
variation.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
M5 <- lm(log(price) ~ log(weight) + cut + clarity, data = diamonds)

anova(M4, M5)
```

b.  

Model under H0 (M4): log(price)∼log(weight)+cut  
Model under H1 (M5): log(price)∼log(weight)+cut+clarity

$F = \frac{(RSS_{M4} - RSS_{M5}) / (df_{M4} - df_{M5})}{RSS_{M5} / df_{M5}}$  

The variable clarity has 2 levels, so it adds 2−1=1 parameters. $df_1=1$ Residual degrees of freedom.
for M5: Total observations n=607. M5 has parameters: intercept + log(weight) + cut(2) + clarity(1) = 5 parameters. $df_2 = 607-5 = 602$.
Therefore, under $H_0$, $F∼F(1,602)$  
observed F = 941  
p-value less than 0.001  
reject $H_0$ 
There is very strong evidence that including clarity significantly improves the model for predicting log(price), after accounting for log(weight) and cut. Clarity is an important predictor of diamond prices and should be retained in the model.

c.  

Yes, we could have used a two-sided t-test. From the ANOVA table, we see that the difference in degrees of freedom between M4 and M5 is 1. This means the variable clarity adds only one single parameter to the model. When comparing two nested models that differ by exactly one parameter, the partial F-test is mathematically equivalent to a two-sided t-test for that single coefficient.
